_comment: Landing pages for search, at /gifts/<slug>/. Each one is written, not generated: if a page would only be a find-and-replace of another it does not belong here, and Google's scaled-content rules would bin it anyway. Every entry carries its own headline, opening, body, game list, giving advice, honest 'is it right' section and its own three questions, plus an example family that gets drawn on the page. English only, because a machine-translated landing page is worse than none. Not in the menu: the hub at /gifts/ and the sitemap are how they are found. Add one by adding an entry; the build does the rest.

pages.title: A birthday gift for a 7 year old who has everything
pages.description: A video game with the 7 year old as the hero and their own family as the opponents. Free to try in a minute, no photos asked for, and it arrives the same day you pay.
pages.h1: A birthday present for a seven year old who has everything
pages.lede: Seven is the age where the toys stop landing. They have the bricks, they have the scooter, and the thing they actually want is to be the main character.
pages.angle: Make them the main character, not the audience.
body: This is a video game where they are. Their name goes up in lights on the title screen, and the people they know turn up as the ones to beat: Dad in the water balloon fight, their sister in the back seat battle, and the dog refereeing.

Seven is a good age for it. They can read the screen without help, they can win without an adult taking over, and they are old enough to care that it is their name up there and not a character from something they already watch. It plays on the phone or the tablet that is already in the house, so there is nothing to set up on the day.
pages.playsIntro: Five games, each against a different person in the family. Every one takes about three minutes, so a seven year old gets to the end of the whole thing in one sitting.
plays: Paddle Battle. A goal-line duel on a pitch with a crowd behind it. First to three.
Water Balloon Fight. The back garden, a fence, a washing line, and whoever is in the other half getting soaked.
Back Seat Battle. The argument about who is over the line, settled in a car with the road rolling away behind it.
Dinner Dash. Catching what comes off the counter. Their favourite food is worth the most, and the sprouts cost them.
The final battle. One last challenge with someone from the family on their side, then their name up in lights.
pages.day: You get a web address that is theirs alone. Open it on whatever is nearest and hand it over: it goes straight to the title screen with their name on it, which is the bit worth filming. If you want something to unwrap, the printed poster of that title screen arrives in the post and goes in the card, or on the wall afterwards.
pages.ask: Their first name, the people who should be in it, and two or three details only your family would know: what they love, what they always say, the joke that gets repeated at the table. No photos, no surname, no age, no school. Ten minutes of thinking is enough, and there is a form that asks it all in order.
pages.suitsTitle: Is it right for a seven year old?
pages.suits: Yes, for most. They read fast enough for the screens, and the games forgive a bad round. Two things to know honestly: it is a browser game rather than a console game, so it will not survive a comparison with the graphics on a PlayStation, and a child who is genuinely obsessed with one particular game franchise may want that franchise instead. What it has that those do not is their own name, their own family and their own jokes.
faq: How long will it keep them busy?

Ten to twenty minutes to play the whole thing through the first time. Most play it again straight away, then hand it to whoever is in the room, which is the part that usually lasts longer than the game.
Can their friends play it at the party?
Yes. Party mode is on the first screen: pick how many are playing and each one takes a turn against the birthday child while the rest watch. It ends on a results board with a champion.
What if their name is spelled differently?
Tell us the spelling you want and that is what goes up in lights. If it comes back wrong, say so and we will fix it and send a new link, at no charge.

pages.title: A Christmas gift for a 10 year old who is hard to buy for
pages.description: A Christmas video game starring the 10 year old, with their family as the opponents. Free to try, nothing to install, and a printed poster to put under the tree.
pages.h1: A Christmas present for a ten year old who is hard to buy for
pages.lede: Ten is old enough to know what everything costs and young enough to still want a surprise. That is a narrow gap to buy into.
pages.angle: Something to unwrap, and something to play.
body: A game with them in it lands in that gap, because there is nothing to compare it against. The title screen says their name. Their brother is in the back seat battle, their best friend is in the dinner dash, and the ending has them winning in front of everybody, with the snow coming down and their name up in lights.

Ten year olds are also the age that notices effort. A present that somebody clearly wrote down details for, right down to the thing they always say at dinner, reads differently from a present that was in stock.
pages.playsIntro: Five games, each against a different person, and a Christmas ending. At ten they will want to beat all five in one go, then go back for the ones they lost.
plays: Paddle Battle. Goal to goal against whoever in the family claims to be good at sport.
Water Balloon Fight. The garden in summer, which is funnier in December.
Back Seat Battle. Every long drive your family has ever had, in thirty seconds.
Dinner Dash. Their favourite food worth triple, and the thing they refuse to eat costing them points.
The final battle. A team-up with somebody from the family, then the Christmas ending with the snow coming down.
pages.day: The trouble with a digital present is that there is nothing under the tree. The poster fixes that: a printed arcade poster of their own title screen, their name in lights, posted to you in time to wrap. They open the poster, you hand them the link, and the game is already waiting. The game itself arrives the day you pay, so it is never too late for that part; only a printed poster needs time for the post.
pages.ask: Their first name, who else is in it, and a few things only your house knows: the catchphrase, the food they love, the argument that never ends. No photos and no surnames. If you are ordering as a surprise, everything you send stays between us and you.
pages.suitsTitle: Is it right for a ten year old?
pages.suits: Usually. Ten is the top end of the sweet spot: old enough to find the jokes funny and young enough not to have decided that pixel art is for babies. If they play a lot of big-budget games, sell it as what it is, a present with them in it, rather than as a game that competes with those. For a child heading for thirteen, the poster tends to matter more than the games do.
faq: When do I need to order for Christmas?

The game arrives the same day you pay, so any time before Christmas morning. If you want a printed poster under the tree, allow for the post in your own country and order in the first week of December.
Can it be a surprise from Santa?
Yes. Nothing arrives by email to the child, only to you. What you do with the link after that is your business.
Can their cousins be in it too?
Up to eight people, and they do not have to live in the same house. Cousins, a best friend, a teacher, a coach and the pet all fit.

pages.title: A gift for a child who loves football and already has a ball
pages.description: A video game where the football-mad child is the hero and their family are the opponents, played on a pitch with a crowd. No club badges, no real players, free to try.
pages.h1: A gift for a child who loves football and already has a ball
pages.lede: There is a limit to how many footballs one child needs, and most families passed it years ago.
pages.angle: A pitch, a crowd, and the people they argue with about football.
body: The games here are played on a pitch in front of a crowd, against the people they actually argue with about football. Paddle Battle is a goal-line duel with their dad in the other net.

We do not use club names, crests, kits or real players, on purpose. Nothing in the game belongs to anybody else, nothing dates when a player transfers, and it will not go stale when they change their mind about who they support in two years. The shirt colour is theirs to pick, which is usually all the loyalty a seven year old needs.
pages.playsIntro: Five games. Two of them are sport, and the other three are the family, which is where the shouting comes from.
plays: Paddle Battle. On the pitch, goal to goal, with a crowd and a centre circle. First to three.
Water Balloon Fight. The back garden, and no, being fast does not save you.
Back Seat Battle. The drive home from training, condensed.
Dinner Dash. The meal before the match. Their favourite is worth triple.
The final battle. A team-up with their dad or their coach, then the ending with the crowd on its feet.
pages.day: It arrives as a web address of their own, so you can send it the moment you want to. If it is for a birthday, hand it over on a phone and let them see their own name on the title screen with the crowd behind it. The printed poster works well for this one, because it looks like a match poster and it ends up on the bedroom wall next to the real ones.
pages.ask: Their first name, their shirt colour, who else is in it, and a couple of football details we can use: the position they play, the thing the coach always shouts, who they claim to be better than. First names only, no clubs required, and no photos.
pages.suitsTitle: Is it right for a football-mad child?
pages.suits: It is right if what they love is playing and arguing about it. It is not a football simulator and it does not pretend to be: there is no licensed team, no career mode and no squad to manage. If they want a game where they are Haaland, this is not it. If they want a game where they beat their dad and their coach, and their own name is on the screen, it is.
faq: Can you put their club in it?

No, and that is deliberate. Crests, kits and player names belong to other people, and a game full of them would have to be taken down. The shirt colour is yours to choose and everything else in the game is genuinely theirs.
Is it a football game?
One of the five is played on a pitch. The rest are the family ones: the garden, the car, the dinner table and the final battle. The football is the setting more than the sport.
Can the coach be in it?
Yes. Coach is one of the roles, alongside teacher, cousin, best friend and the usual family. Up to eight people in total.

pages.title: A birthday gift for a niece or nephew, from the aunt or uncle
pages.description: A personalized video game starring your niece or nephew, with their family in it and you as one of the opponents. First names are all you need, and no photos.
pages.h1: A birthday present for a niece or nephew
pages.lede: The job of an aunt or an uncle is to turn up with the thing the parents would not have thought of, and then leave.
pages.angle: First names are enough, and you can send it from anywhere.
body: This is that present. A game where they are the hero, their own family are the ones to beat, and you are in it too: Auntie is one of the roles, with her own line of trash talk before the game starts.

It is also the easiest kind of present to buy from a distance. You need their first name and a few details you probably already know, and it arrives as a web address you can send on the day from wherever you are, which is useful when you are the relative who lives three hours away or in another country.
pages.playsIntro: Five games, each against somebody different. You choose who turns up in which one.
plays: Paddle Battle. A goal-line duel. Put yourself in this one if you fancy losing publicly.
Water Balloon Fight. The garden, the fence and the dog getting in the way.
Back Seat Battle. Brother and sister, one seat, an obvious outcome.
Dinner Dash. Their favourite food, worth triple points.
The final battle. A team-up at the end, which is a good place for an aunt to be on the right side for once.
pages.day: You get a link of their own. Send it by message on the morning, put it in a card, or send the printed poster ahead so there is something to open while you are on the phone. Nothing needs installing at their end, and nobody needs an account, which matters when the person opening it is seven and the person supervising is busy.
pages.askTitle: What you need to know about them
pages.ask: Their first name, who else should be in it, and two or three details: what they are into at the moment, what they always say, who they fight with about what. If you are not sure of a detail, leave it out. An empty answer is better than a wrong one, and we would rather write five jokes that land than eight that half do.
pages.suitsTitle: Is it right coming from an aunt or uncle?
pages.suits: It is, and it has one advantage over a present from the parents: you can be in it. The one thing to check is whether the parents mind their own first names being used, because Mum and Dad usually appear as opponents. Nothing beyond first names is ever asked for, and nothing about the child is stored once the game is built.
faq: Do I need to ask their parents first?
For the details, no, first names and a couple of jokes are enough. It is worth a word if you want a surprise that involves the parents playing along on the day.
Can I be in it?
Yes. Auntie and Uncle are both roles, with their own lines. Up to eight people fit in one game.
What if I get a detail wrong?
Tell us and we will fix it and send a new link, once, at no charge. Better still, leave a detail out rather than guessing.

pages.title: A gift from grandparents that is not another toy
pages.description: A video game with your grandchild as the hero and you in it as an opponent. Nothing to install, nothing to learn, and it arrives the same day you pay.
pages.h1: A present from grandparents that is not another toy
pages.lede: The house is full of toys and the grandchild is full of opinions. What they have not got is a game with their granny in it.
pages.angle: You are in it, and there is nothing to install.
body: That is what this is. They are the hero, and you turn up as one of the people they have to beat, cardigan and all, with a line of your own before the game starts. Granny and Grandad are both roles, and you can decide whether you are easy to beat.

The other reason grandparents buy it is that it survives the day. It is not a toy that gets left in a corner by February. It is a web address that plays on any phone in the house, and it has your name in it as well as theirs.
pages.playsIntro: Five games, three minutes each, each against a different person in the family.
plays: Paddle Battle. Goal to goal. A good one to be in if you want to be beaten fairly.
Water Balloon Fight. The garden, and the dog making a nuisance of itself.
Back Seat Battle. The long drive, and who is over the line.
Dinner Dash. Catching dinner. Their favourite is worth triple, and whatever they refuse to eat costs them.
The final battle. One last challenge with Granny or Grandad on their side, then their name in lights.
pages.day: We email you a web address. You tap it, or you send it on to their parents to open on the day. There is no app, no download, no account and no password. If you would rather have something in your hands, the printed poster of their title screen comes in the post and can go in a card or on their wall.
pages.ask: Their first name, who else goes in the game, and a few details you will know better than anyone: what they love, what they always say, what they are like at the dinner table. We never ask for photographs, surnames, ages, schools or addresses. The form is short and asks one thing at a time.
pages.suitsTitle: Do I need to be good with computers?
pages.suits: No. You answer a few questions in a form, the way you would fill in an address, and we do the rest. Nothing is installed on your machine and nothing is downloaded. If you can open an email and tap a link, you can give this present. If you would rather talk to a person, write to hello@happyherogames.com and one will answer.
faq: Will it work on my grandchild's tablet?
Any phone, tablet, laptop or computer with a web browser. Nothing to download and nothing to install.
Can I be in it more than once?
You appear as one of the opponents, and you can be the one who helps them at the end as well. Granny and Grandad can both be in the same game.
What if I make a mistake in the form?
Tell us what is wrong and we will fix it and send a new link. There is no charge for that, and it costs nothing to change.

pages.title: A Father's Day gift from the kids that is not socks
pages.description: A video game where Dad is the hero and the children are the ones to beat. Their jokes, his catchphrase, and a printed poster for the wall if you want one.
pages.h1: A Father's Day present from the kids that is not socks
pages.lede: He does not want socks, he does not want another mug, and he definitely does not want a lie-in he will not be allowed to have.
pages.angle: This time he is the hero and they are the ones to beat.
body: Turn it round: this time Dad is the hero and the children are the ones he has to beat. His name goes up in lights, his catchphrase goes into the game, and the whole thing is his family, his food and his lines, which is usually where it stops being a present and starts being an argument.

It works on the phone in his pocket, and it is the kind of thing that gets played at the table on the day rather than put in a drawer. Two people can play on one keyboard if he wants to settle it properly.
pages.playsIntro: Five games, each against one of the children, and an ending with his name in lights.
plays: Paddle Battle. Goal to goal against whichever child claims to be better at sport.
Water Balloon Fight. The garden. He will lose this one and it will be replayed.
Back Seat Battle. The seat argument, from the other side for once.
Dinner Dash. His favourite food worth triple, and whatever the children make him eat costing him.
The final battle. Dad and one of the children on the same side for once, then his name in lights.
pages.day: Open the link at breakfast and hand him the phone. The title screen says his name, the children are lined up beside him, and the first opponent is whichever one of them talks the most. If you want something to give him, the printed poster of that title screen arrives in the post and is the right size for a desk or a shed wall.
pages.ask: His first name or what the children call him, the children's names, and the details that make it his: the phrase he repeats, the food he will not share, the thing he is convinced he is brilliant at. First names only. No photographs and nothing about the children beyond what goes in the game.
pages.suitsTitle: Is it right for Father's Day?
pages.suits: It suits a dad who will play along, which is most of them when their own children are in it. It does not suit somebody who would rather not be the centre of attention for ten minutes, and it is not a serious game for a serious gamer. The right expectation is a good ten minutes at the table, a poster he keeps, and a video the family ends up sending round.
faq: Can the children choose what he is called?
Yes. Whatever they call him is what goes on the screen, whether that is Dad, Daddy, Pops or his first name.
Can it be from more than one child?
Up to eight people fit in a game, so all the children can be in it, and Mum and the dog too.
How late can I leave it?
The game arrives the same day you pay, so the night before is fine. Only a printed poster needs time for the post.
